items.title: Midori Hirano (Interview)
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we’re listening to Midori Hirano, a Japanese composer and pianist based in Berlin. The last time we recommended her music was in 2021. She uses synth and piano to create electroacoustic pieces that reflect her classical training as well as interest in more experimental compositional techniques. Her latest record is a new score for , the 1990 film by Nietzchka Keene set in Iceland and starring Björk. Reflecting on the process of making the score, she told us, “I think this film has a lot of ambiguity showing different kinds of emotions and you can’t really define who is good or bad actually. And I think that electronic sounds are well suited to expressing subtle aspects of human psychology, while an acoustic instrument like the piano, the nature of the instrument can be quite strong, so I feel it can sometimes limit the kind of impression or feeling it creates.” We’re also revisiting her 2020 record, , whose piano pieces are complex and processed through a range of effects. A conversation with Midori follows the streaming links.

What’s your earliest memory of music?

When I was growing up in Japan in the ‘80s, it was still the bubble era, and there were many children around me who were taking piano lessons.

So whenever I went to play at neighbor’s house, I often heard someone playing the piano. But at the same time, my grandparents bought my brother and me a Super Famicom, which had just been released back then. I often played games like Super Mario with my brother and friends, and the music from those games gradually became embedded in my memory, without me even realizing it. So when I think back on it, both the sound of the piano and the sounds of video games are equally part of my earliest musical memories.

How did you get started with piano? What was the first piece that you learned that felt like a real accomplishment?

As I mentioned above, so many children around me were taking piano lessons when I was a child, so I just became interested in playing it as well. Even in my small hometown, there seemed to be someone giving piano lessons on almost every block in my neighbourhood at that time. But before I started playing piano when I was around six, we had a small pump organ at home, and I remember just playing around on it, making whatever sound I felt like.

I don’t really remember what the first piece I managed to play properly was, but I think it was probably one of those standard little pieces by Bach or Mozart.

What were the artists/albums that early on helped point you in the direction of your own sound?

When I started making electronic music in early 2000s, glitch and all kinds of experimental electronic music were thriving at the time. So I’m sure I was inspired by a lot of those music. But if I had to pick just one, it would have to be Tujiko Noriko’s , which was released on Mego. I found it very refreshing how freely field recordings, sampled sounds, and noise were arranged, yet somehow they all came together well as a pop song.

is an interesting blend of synth and piano. How do you think about using either instrument – does a musical idea occur to you along with the instrument, or do you tend to find the musical idea once at the instrument?

It really depends, but when speaking about producing the score for , I naturally came to the idea of using synthesizers for most of the score, and the piano should stay as occasional use, after watching the film. Because I think this film has a lot of ambiguity showing different kinds of emotions and you can’t really define who is good or bad actually. And I think that electronic sounds are well suited to expressing subtle aspects of human psychology, while an acoustic instrument like the piano, the nature of the instrument can be quite strong, so I feel it can sometimes limit the kind of impression or feeling it creates. So I kept the use of the piano to a minimum, using it instead at key points in the story, and I think it worked quite well.

What was your studio setup for ? What instruments/gear/software did you use to make the album?

Since the music was specifically composed to be performed live as a solo piece, the setup was quite minimal as listed below:

- Small modular setup - Mutable Instruments’ oscillator Plaits, Doepfer’s LFO A-145 and Morphagene by Make Noise

- Strymon Bigsky reverb pedal

Around 60% of the album was made using only with MiniFreak, with 9-10 different presets. I altered their sound characteristics using the filters. For track 8 “Take Me With You,“ I used only Plaits as the sound source. I connected a sine-wave LFO to Plaits’ Level input and used the LFO’s dynamics and intervals to slowly evolve the timbre.

And at the beginning of the track 9 “Mother’s Path,“ I kept a piano phrase recorded with Morphagene looping, while using its granular capabilities to significantly transform the sound. All sounds from both modules were routed through the Bigsky.

To produce the album, I recorded everything in Abelton Live and made some subtle EQ adjustments there, while also adding a minimum amount of reverb using Valhalla plugins. As I was already happy with my initial compositions I’ve made for the premiere concert, I tried not to change them too much and instead focused more on mixing, especially with the last track “Forever In The Sky“ where I used Plugin Boutique’s Stereo Savage to expand and deepen the stereo panning.

What's it like composing for a film, versus creating your own original music?

When composing for a film, you usually have a director who often has certain musical ideas that you need to realize. But when creating your own music, you can do whatever you want, so this is obviously the main difference. But for me, sometimes having musical limitations or being asked to work within someone else’s ideas can actually help me find a new way of approaching things, both technically and creatively.

But the situation with was a little different from a usual scoring project, as the music was composed genuinely for live performance. I had complete creative freedom, while the music of course still needed to work well with the story. That was actually the only real limitation I had, and it gave me a lot of inspiration. I’m very thankful to VIERNULVIER for giving me this special opportunity.

How do you discover new music these days? Any recent notable finds?

I often discover new music while exploring Bandcamp or some random websites, or otherwise at concerts or record stores. The record I recently stumbled upon and bought is Helen Money’s . This album is already a couple of years old, but I’m happy I found it now, thanks to the shop Bis Aufs Messer in Berlin. I really enjoyed the beautiful, massive sound of her cello.

Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.

I think everyone has a different idea of what makes someone underrated, but if I had to name one, I’d say Natalie Beridze. There’s always a real strength at the core of her sound, and at times, it also has a sense of spaciousness and warmth. I enjoy almost everything she makes.

What are you working on next?

Since I’m releasing two albums this year, and I’ve released quite a few albums and worked on several scoring projects over the past few years as well, I feel like I’d like to focus more on playing live as much as possible for a while, rather than making new music.

items.title: Shinichi Atobe
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Shinichi Atobe, a Japanese electronic musician from Saitama. We’ve recommended his music afewtimesbefore. He’s been making quality techno/house music, beasting in the underground since the start of the millennium. In a conversation with Tone Glow, he said, “I started making techno when I was 27. At the time, I was working as a security guard. I saved up money to buy a Prophet 600. I was listening to a variety of techno music.” We’re playing his latest album, , which came out in March. It carries on his style of laid back techno, with drums keeping the pace and synths conveying his signature form of energized calm. We’re also playing from 2018, which to our ears is his magnum opus.

Have a fantastic weekend.

items.title: TKB (Guest rec from Ryan Mandelbaum)
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we have a guest recommendation from , a writer and occasional DJ, whose newsletter is a valuable source of thoughtful curation and honest reflections on the world of experimental sound.

Today I’d like to shine a light on an artist who is, in my opinion, one of the most brilliant and overlooked minds currently operating in the world of ambient and experimental adjacent sound, someone I recommend whenever I am given the chance: Timothy K. Brown aka TKB.

Trying to describe TKB’s sound in terms of musical reference points is nearly impossible because, simply put, there is nothing out there quite like it. It is a sound that I’d best describe as elemental – as if he somehow discovered a method for recording the ancient music of the earth itself, the essential and imperceptible melody that vibrates through everyone and everything. TKB’s entire discography is well worth delving into, but his three most recent releases (each respectively finding their way to the very top of my year end lists) are all perfect launching points.

is an otherworldly and at times disorienting listen filled with some of the most unique textures I’ve ever heard. Jon Hassell, Zoviet France, and even the work of James Ferraro and Spencer Clarke are the closest comparisons I can think of, but again… TKB’s world is entirely his own. released just a few months later on World of Knots, takes a much more rhythmic approach, its exoskeletal rhythmic patterns far removed from any sense human involvement, rather resembling those found in nature – the fluttering of moth wings, the whisper of wind through leaves, the mating call of crickets dancing in and out of phase with each other.

is easily TKB’s most serene work yet. While it might be absent of the jittery and at times anxious sense of constant motion present in much of his work, it is nonetheless defined by the same sense of dark mystery, as if one is peering into the very deepest part of the night, and given access to its most forbidden secrets. Don’t let this description scare you off though – this is possibly the most beautiful album of the year, perfect to drift off to. A much needed corner of serenity in a constantly overstimulating world.

items.title: Across the Horizon Ep. 71: Lara Somogyi
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
On today’s episode of Across the Horizon, host Bob Holmes of the band SUSS is joined by Lara Somogyi. Lara is a harpist and composer who recently released an album on Mercury KX Records. They talk about her new music as well as the playlist of ambient music that she brought to the show, including Ólafur Arnalds, Clarice Jensen, Steve Reich, Koki Nakano, and much more.

For Flow State, we’re listening to two albums by Somogyi, whose music has appeared on many of our mixes and whom we featured last year. First up is the new record, , on which she passes her harp through a medley of effects pedals. She says on the show, “I’ve been listening to a lot of music that shifts time for me, or makes me feel time physically. I started making the record because I was curious about time… I discovered I experience it through sensory markers rather than through numerical markers.” We’re also playing from last year, a collaboration with Joshua Tree-born pianist Jean-Michel Blais. Included in our daily playlist for paying subscribers is her unmissable covers of “Running Up That Hill” and “Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence,” among other selections.

items.title: Flow State Episode 345
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today’s mix opens with a beautiful new track from Isik Kural, followed by new ambient by Maxime Denuc and elijah jamal asani. There are instrumentals by M. Sage and K. Leimer, and then a long new ambient piece by Windy & Carl (who have a new album out). There’s a saxophone-led instrumental by Cole Pulice and then a guitar-led slow burn jam by Time Wharp. We play a couple new low-key techno tracks by Mammo and Shinichi Atobe, followed by one of Patrick Cowley’s reissued HI-NRG pieces. The last two tracks are a triumphant piece by Akusmi and a sample that may be familiar. We hope you enjoy.

items.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we’re listening to Ryuichi Sakamoto, a Japanese composer and pianist from Tokyo. We’ve recommended him a fewtimesbefore. The occasion for today’s rec is last week’s publication of of Sakamoto’s memoir, . The book is a twofer: it’s the English translations (by Sam Bett) of two autobiographical works by Sakamoto, the first from 2009 and the second from 2023, the year he passed away. We’re playing two piano records released around the time of those texts – 2009’s . Sakamoto studied piano intensively in elementary school and recalled being “shocked” by Debussy in junior high:

I was browsing through one of my uncle’s collections of records when I found Debussy’s String Quartet…. I snuck it home with me and played it on the stereo entertainment system, this huge thing built like a piece of furniture and covered up with lace. What I heard next was a total shock to me. This was different from any other music I’d heard before. Nothing like the Bach or Beethoven I liked. The second that I heard it, I was mesmerized. My affinity for Debussy was so strong that it blurred my sense of self. I started thinking of him, despite being dead for ages, as if his life and mine were one and the same. I thought I was the reincarnation of Debussy. It made me question where I lived and why I could speak Japanese. I even practiced the man’s signature, filling multiple notebook pages with

We wish you a great start to your week.
